title: Why Academics *Still* Matter for Long-Term Flourishing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. addresses an apparent paradox: academic achievement is not the best predictor of a flourishing life, yet schools should still concentrate on academic mastery for every student. His reasoning is that the effort of mastering any discipline, whether writing, biology, music, or running, produces noncognitive byproducts such as perseverance, focus, curiosity, and reflection. He describes the teacher as animated by three loves (the discipline, the young people, and the challenge of helping them master it) and insists that teaching content, not life lessons in general, is the teacher's assigned slice of a child's broader formation. He sets this against a prevailing view that skills can be divorced from knowledge, and ends by deferring the question of measurement to a later post, noting that bad tests tied to rewards and punishments are the real problem.
points: Mastering a hard discipline is itself the vehicle for noncognitive growth, so schools do not need to choose between rigor and character.
The teacher's job description is to teach the subject, with lessons about life arriving as a byproduct of that struggle rather than as a replacement for it.
Stuart names three loves a teacher needs: love of the discipline, love of the young people, and love of the challenge of bringing the two together.
He criticizes the idea that skill can be separated from knowledge and mastery as an exaltation of the present moment over inherited human knowledge.
He flags that the real problem with testing is low-quality tests attached to carrots and sticks, not measurement itself.
quotes: Because the work of mastering something — be it writing or biology or physical fitness or music — has, as its byproduct, the noncognitive fruits that do seem most integral to a flourishing life — things like perseverance and focus and curiosity and reflection. When you work to improve your running performance, you get increased focus, resilience, and engagement as a result.

The disciplines — of economics and mathematics and research and painting — are wonderful because they are both hard and fruitful. Mastering them absolutely is something one aspires to for a lifetime, but mastering them bit by bit is something we invite our students into each school year.

The teacher, then, must be animated by three loves: love for the discipline, love for the young people, and love for the challenge of helping young people master the discipline. (Thank you to John Strebe’s book on mathematics for first introducing me to these.)

If all I have done is taught them a great deal about life, then what I’ve done is misallocated the time I was given. Indeed, my job description is not to teach the kids about life — it is to teach them about world history.

This is a bit of an off-tune message in a world obsessed with the mistaken notion that skill can somehow be divorced from knowledge and mastery. It seems the general sense today that knowledge and mastery and the disciplines are not as important as one’s individual desires and preferences and choices.
I’m still working on that. But eventually, we need to have a talk about measurement. Because it’s not tests that are the problem: it’s crappy tests attached to carrots and sticks (especially sticks).
